notes.meaning: Christian masters are commanded to treat their servants with justice and fairness. They are reminded that they have their own Master in heaven to whom they must give an account. Remembering God's authority over them should lead them to treat others with equity and kindness.

Believers are urged to pray regularly and not give up. They must stay spiritually alert, keeping their minds awake against laziness and distraction. Every prayer should also include heartfelt thanks to God for His blessings.

Paul asks the church to pray especially for him and his fellow ministers. He asks God to open a door for their preaching so they can share the mystery of Christ, the gospel message that was hidden for generations. Even while chained in prison, Paul cares most about getting the good news out to others.

Paul wants them to pray that he will make the gospel message clear and understandable. Even an experienced apostle felt the weight of preaching God's truth as faithfully as he ought to do. Ministers depend on God's help to speak with bold clarity.

Christians must act with wisdom and good judgment toward outsiders who do not yet believe. Living with honesty and care keeps the gospel from being brought into disrepute. Believers are also told to redeem the time, making the most of every chance to do good and point others to Christ.

Believers should speak in a gracious and pleasant way at all times. Like salt that adds good flavor to food and keeps it from spoiling, their words should be pure, wise, and helpful. Speaking this way helps Christians know how to give a gentle and fitting answer to anyone who asks about their faith.

Paul describes Tychicus as a dearly loved brother, a faithful helper, and a fellow servant in the Lord. Instead of writing every personal update in the letter, Paul sends Tychicus in person to report all the news. The church could trust him completely to share how Paul was doing in Rome.

Paul sent Tychicus with the specific goal of bringing news and comforting the believers. Hearing that Paul remained joyful and steadfast in his trials would strengthen the Colossians in their own difficulties. Mutual concern between believers brings deep encouragement in hard times.

Onesimus travels alongside Tychicus as a faithful and dearly loved Christian brother who came from Colossae. Although Onesimus was a runaway slave, the gospel made him a transformed brother in Christ, showing that social standing does not divide God's family. Together, these two men were ready to report everything happening with Paul in Rome.

Aristarchus, who was locked up in prison alongside Paul, sends his greetings to the church. Paul also sends greetings from Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, whom Paul had once refused to travel with after an earlier failure. Having fully forgiven Mark, Paul warmly commands the believers to welcome him if he visits.

A believer named Jesus, also called by the Roman name Justus, sends his greetings as well. These three men were the only Jewish Christians working alongside Paul in Rome, and their loyalty brought him great personal comfort. Their faithful partnership gave Paul relief while many other local opponents worked against him.

Epaphras, a minister from Colossae, sends his greetings while staying with Paul. He is described as wrestling and working hard in constant prayer for the believers back home. His deep prayer was that they would stand firm, reach spiritual maturity, and be completely confident in doing everything God wants.

Paul testifies that Epaphras worked with great zeal and concern for the Colossian believers. His loving care also reached out to the neighboring churches in Laodicea and Hierapolis. Epaphras cared deeply that all these local congregations stayed safe from false teachings.

Luke, the doctor who wrote the Gospel and the book of Acts, sends his warm greetings to the church. He cared for Paul's health during his travels and imprisonment. Demas also sends greetings, though Scripture later records that he sadly deserted Paul because he loved the things of this world.

Paul asks the Colossians to pass on greetings to the believers living in neighboring Laodicea. He specifically mentions Nymphas and the local congregation that met in this home. Before dedicated church buildings existed, early Christians gathered in private homes to worship and encourage one another.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars read the Greek name as feminine (Nympha) based on early manuscripts, concluding that the host of the house church was a Christian woman.

notes.meaning: Paul gives instructions for this letter to be read out loud to the Colossian church and then passed to the church in Laodicea. In return, the Colossians were to get and read the letter coming from Laodicea. Sharing letters in this way allowed the apostles' teachings to guide and strengthen multiple congregations.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars believe the letter from Laodicea was the circular letter now known as the Epistle to the Ephesians, which was passed from church to church in the region.

notes.meaning: The believers are told to deliver a personal message to Archippus, urging him to finish the work the Lord had given him to do. This reminder was meant to encourage him in his ministry rather than tear him down. Every task given by Christ is an important trust that requires steady faithfulness to complete.

Paul adds his final greeting with his own hand to prove that the letter is genuinely from him. He asks the believers to remember his chains, which serves as a reminder to pray for him and stand firm in the gospel he suffered for. He closes by praying that God's grace—His unearned favor and help—will remain with them all.
